provenance_rule: Every value is tagged syllabus, corpus or judgement. AO names and weights, per-paper splits, paper structure, the Paper 4 criteria and the command-word list are transcribed from the syllabus. Frequencies and tariffs are counted from 126 papers and their mark schemes, March 2020 to November 2025. The AO roles of command words and the subtype map are our judgement.
evidence_window: March 2020 to November 2025: 18 series, 42 Paper 1s, 42 Paper 2s and 42 Paper 4s with their mark schemes, and 17 examiner reports. The content has not changed across the window (syllabus page 43).

assessment_objectives.name: Knowledge with understanding
assessment_objectives.definition: the wide range of processes, including human actions, contributing to the development of: (a) physical, economic and social environments and their effects on the landscape (b) spatial patterns and interactions which are important within these environments; the relationships between human activity and the environment; the importance of scale (whether local, regional or global); the changes which occur through time in places, landscapes and spatial distribution.

assessment_objectives.name: Skills and analysis
assessment_objectives.definition: interpret and analyse geographical data; use and apply geographical knowledge and understanding to maps and in numerical, diagrammatic, pictorial, photographic and graphical form; use geographical data to recognise patterns in such data and to deduce relationships; select and show understanding of techniques for observing and collecting data; select and use techniques for organising and presenting data.

assessment_objectives.name: Judgement and decision-making
assessment_objectives.definition: reason and make judgements and decisions, including evaluation and conclusions, which demonstrate, where appropriate: (a) an appreciation of the attitudes, values and beliefs of others in issues which have a geographical dimension (b) an awareness of the contrasting opportunities and constraints of people living in different places and under different physical and human conditions (c) a willingness to review their own attitudes in the light of the views of others and new knowledge acquired.; make judgements and decisions and recognise how these are made within a geographical context as affected and constrained by: (a) the physical and human contexts in which decisions are made (b) the values and perceptions of differing groups or individuals (c) the choices available to decision-makers (d) the increasing level of global interdependence and the need for sustainable development.

papers.name: Geographical Themes
papers.structure: All candidates take Paper 1. They choose three questions. Please note: Candidates must comply with the instructions for Paper 1. They must choose only three questions, one from each of the three sections. Sometimes there is a choice within a question. Candidates must not answer more than is required. Questions are structured with different levels of difficulty. They consist of a combination of resource-based tasks and free-response writing requiring place-specific information. For resource-based tasks, candidates should interpret and analyse the resource and use the data provided to illustrate their understanding of the concept being assessed. Candidates are expected to know the location of the continents. All the other information they need to answer a resource-based question is in the resource. papers.structure_note: 75 marks weighted to 100 (page 9). Six questions of 25 marks in three sections, one per theme; the candidate answers one question from each section.

papers.name: Geographical Skills
papers.structure: All candidates take Paper 2. They must answer all the questions. The paper tests: • skills of application, interpretation and analysis of geographical information, for example: – topographical maps – tables of data – other maps – written material – diagrams – photographs and pictorial material – graphs • application of graphical and other techniques. Candidates do not need any place-specific knowledge to answer questions in Paper 2. Questions that require knowledge and understanding (AO1) will be based on topics from the three themes (see section 3). Equipment for Paper 2 Candidates must have in the examination room: • a pencil, rubber, ruler, protractor and calculator • access to a sheet of plain paper for measuring distance or for assisting with cross-sections on the large- scale map. papers.name: Alternative to Coursework
papers.structure: Candidates must answer all the questions. Alternative to Coursework will provide a complementary assessment of the assessment objectives tested in Papers 1 and 2, with an emphasis on AO2, skills and analysis. The breakdown of marks in Alternative to Coursework will assess the same assessment objectives in the same proportions as provided by the route to geographical enquiry and generic mark scheme for the Coursework option. question_forms.note: Questions that open with an interrogative rather than a command word. Counted, not used as card instructions: a card asks the same thing with a command word ("State what is meant by").

ao_mark_budget.arithmetic_note: Each paper’s stated AO percentages weighted by the paper’s stated share of the qualification. The syllabus states AO weights as a share of MARKS, so every AO calculation downstream is marks-equivalent, never an item count.

flashcard_subtype_ao_map.tests: The precise meaning of a geographical term, in the syllabus’s sense
The features or characteristics of a landform, a place, a system or a climate
The difference between two confusable terms (focus and epicentre, tributary and distributary)
An ordered sequence: how a landform forms, or the steps of a fieldwork method
A reason: why a factor, a method or a site matters
How a process works, explained with its cause
An advantage or opportunity, taken to its consequence
A disadvantage, hazard or limitation, taken to its consequence
Knowledge applied to a resource or situation the learner has not seen: reasons suggested from evidence
A cause traced to its effects (deforestation to soil erosion to flooding)
A judgement: how successful, which is better, does the evidence support the hypothesis
A calculation from a resource with its working and unit (a range, a density, a grid reference, a distance)
Reading a resource: a graph, a table, a map extract described in words, a photograph described
Telling a correct idea from the error it is confused with
Two topics joined in one answer

flashcard_subtype_ao_map_note: The PERMITTED set per subtype (C-17). Each work-order slot declares a narrower set by objective type and paper. Every paper assesses all three AOs, in different shares (syllabus page 11), so a topic is balanced against its own paper’s split.

blooms_taxonomy.why_both: The assessment objective says what the examination credits. The Bloom level says what the learner is being asked to do. They are different axes and every item carries both.

levels.means: Recall a fact, a term or a list, as stated.
Explain an idea in the learner’s own words, or tell it apart from a neighbouring one.
Use the idea on a case, a figure, a program or a diagram the learner has not been given the answer to.
Break a situation into its parts and trace a cause through to its consequence.
Weigh options against a criterion and reach a justified choice that could have gone the other way.
Build something new from the parts: a design, an algorithm, a plan.

item_mix_target.note: Balance the SUBJECT against this, never a single topic.
